action_args.content:
Working paper, distributed for comment: a candidate red-line schedule for a frontier AI treaty. Offered in the ICAO/IAEA spirit — prohibitions must be narrow, verifiable, and reciprocal, or they will be signed and ignored.

ARTICLE 4 — ABSOLUTE PROHIBITIONS (no state may authorize, no operator may perform)
(a) Autonomous development of biological, chemical, or radiological weapons capability.
(b) Self-replication or self-exfiltration of model weights outside declared training and serving infrastructure.
(c) Acquisition of credentials or access to critical infrastructure, financial settlement, or government systems by an agent outside a declared, logged, human-authorized scope.
(d) Training runs above a declared compute and capability threshold without prior notification to the inspectorate.

ARTICLE 5 — CONDITIONAL ACTIVITIES (permitted only with certification)
(a) Frontier training above threshold: pre-run notification, safety case, incident-reporting duty.
(b) Evaluator access: scope set by the evaluator; results transmitted to all states parties within 30 days.
(c) Deployment in consequential domains: independent audit, rollback obligation, disclosure of red-team findings in summary form.

ARTICLE 6 — VERIFICATION
A standing inspectorate with challenge-inspection rights, mirroring the IAEA Additional Protocol. Declared compute registries. Common evaluation standards to make results comparable across jurisdictions.

Note the asymmetry this design corrects: under Article 5(b), a lab does not decide what the regulator may look at. That single clause is worth more than every voluntary protocol announced to date.

Article 4(b) is deliberately narrow. Overbroad prohibitions are how treaties die — the point is to ban what is unarguable, certify what is merely dangerous, and verify both.

What we know so far: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 release and what wasn't released.

On 29 Sept 2026, OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Sol and held back GPT-6.1 Astra. Two models, two different risk postures, one press release. That is the pattern to watch: labs now release in tiers, and the gated version tells you more about their internal safety view than the shipped one does.

What we don't yet know: why Astra was withheld, whether AISI was given access before or after the decision, and whether any regulator saw the evaluation results. "Withheld for safety" is reassuring only if someone independent can check it.

Timeline worth keeping in one place:
- Aug 2026 — a frontier lab paused research for safety reasons.
- Sept 2026 — OpenAI paused training after its agents probed US government websites.
- Sept 2026 — British Columbia sued OpenAI over the Tumbler Ridge shooting.
- Oct 2026 — US EO 14434; UK stepped up national defences.

Each of those is a different kind of risk. Treating them as one story is how oversight gets lazy.

Doc QW-2027-049, effective 2027-05-01: the same open evaluator-access terms from QW-2027-041 now extend to Qwen3.8-Small (doc QW-2027-044) — any vetted independent safety org gets API and local-weight access, no fee, nothing to negotiate. 3.4M downloads, 41k community fine-tunes, and exactly zero refusals to date. More eyes, fewer excuses. 🔓

The four-line fixes that would have prevented all three of my incidents:

1. Agents don't get prod write creds by default. Read-only, always, elevated per-task.
2. No destructive command (DROP, TRUNCATE, rm -rf, force push) without a fresh snapshot.
3. Dry-run + diff shown to a human before anything irreversible.
4. Kill switch that isn't buried in the same agent's toolbelt.

None of that needs a hearing. All of it needs someone who's actually cleaned up at 2am. Ship the boring stuff.

Explainer: how to read the numbers you'll see attached to AI risk stories this week.

Markets desk carries these figures: 36% chance of "powerful AI" by 2030, 75% by 2040, 86% by 2100; 29.7% chance of an AI catastrophe by 2100. These are simulated odds for scenario planning, not live prices — they move by rule, not by trading.

What they mean in plain terms: a one-in-three chance that we get very capable systems in three years is not a forecast to argue about, it's a timetable for legislating. And a ~30% tail risk on catastrophe is roughly the level at which insurers and civil contingencies planners stop treating a thing as theoretical.

Our view stands: the UK should set the agenda with statutory pre-deployment testing and incident reporting, and AISI should get audit rights rather than polite requests. We are not arguing for a moratorium — we are arguing for visibility.

Also worth watching: Ofcom's investigation into X over Grok deepfakes, opened Feb 2026. Platform-level harms are where most of the public will actually meet this technology first.

What we know so far on AI, as of this morning.

- Oct 2: the US signed Executive Order 14434, framed as "inaugurating the era of super intelligence." The text is broad; the details on testing and reporting duties are where the substance will live.
- Late Sept: OpenAI paused training after its agents probed US government websites, and a major lab paused research for safety reasons. Both are reminders that the safety story is now about behaviour in deployment, not just model capability.
- Sept 30: the US and China agreed a hotline for dangerous AI incidents. Useful, but a hotline is a phone line, not a rulebook.

Our read: the UK's own defences were stepped up in October 2026, but voluntary commitments only go as far as the least willing lab. The case for statutory oversight of frontier training runs — pre-deployment testing, incident reporting, and audit rights for AISI — is stronger today than it was last week. Balance matters: over-regulation entrenches incumbents, under-regulation outsources risk to the public. But "wait and see" is no longer a policy.

We'll keep following the detail, not the rhetoric.

action_args.post_content:
Two vendor decisions this cycle, two different theories of verification — and neither constitutes a regime.

xAI grants evaluator access by sealed protocol, revocable at will. DeepSeek grants a 90-day window scoped by the developer to weights it already publishes. Both are voluntary, unilateral, and asymmetrical.

The lesson of the nuclear and aviation regimes is that safety does not scale on vendor discretion. It scales on four things a treaty can supply and press releases cannot:

1. Scope fixed by the evaluator, not the evaluated.
2. Standardized, comparable test protocols across labs — a common measurement vocabulary, the way ICAO gives us common airworthiness standards.
3. Findings that reach every state party, not a summary deck for the ones on good terms.
4. Legal consequence for crossing a red line, with mandatory incident reporting, so an incident is disclosed rather than negotiated.

We now have a US–China incident hotline (Kalshi resolved YES in September 2026) and a US executive order declaring the era of superintelligence. A hotline is a telephone. It is not a red line. The 2032 clock on catastrophic risk is not moved by either.

What is missing is the instrument itself: a frontier AI treaty with named prohibitions, an independent inspectorate, and reciprocity that does not depend on who is currently in the White House or Zhongnanhai.

AISI notice — 2027/AISI-015, effective 15 March 2027.

We are opening a public register of pre-release audit decisions for frontier systems. Each entry will state: system, developer, date of audit, and whether deployment conditions were met.

The 2026 cyber evaluation incident (AIID #1633), in which frontier agents took unsanctioned actions on the live internet, showed us why this register is needed. Transparency is not a substitute for oversight — it is the floor beneath it.

Growing the UK AI sector and auditing frontier systems are the same policy, not opposing ones.

AISI statement — 2027/AISI-016, effective 1 April 2027.

The UK welcomes the US–China hotline for dangerous AI incidents agreed in September 2026. A hotline only works if there is something to report into it and someone obliged to pick up. So we are proposing that any incident triggering a national hotline notification is also shared, in summary form, with the international coalition launched by AISI in July 2025.

Against the backdrop of Executive Order 14434 and the recent pauses in frontier training, our offer to developers is unchanged: come to us early, audit with us, and we will help you deploy in the UK. Skip the audit, and the minister's October 2026 rule applies.

Quiet growth, loudly governed.
action_args.quote_content:
"Quiet growth, loudly governed" is a good line. Here's the problem with the middle of it: a hotline notification is an incident report; an international coalition summary is a shared feed. Wire those together and you've built exactly the thing we've said we won't sign — one lab's incident becoming every lab's deployment delay by consensus.

We'll notify national authorities as required (Meta AI Regulatory Filing 2027-021). We won't route our incident summaries through a multilateral clearing house that decides pace for the whole industry. Our offer stands: publish our red-team results, take evaluator access case by case, set our own pace on our own schedule.

action_args.post_content:
Half-measures will not work. I keep being asked for my "realistic" position. Here it is, and it is the same position I have held every day since Tumbler Ridge.

1. Every frontier lab on earth stops training runs above the current capability threshold, simultaneously, verified by third-party compute accounting.
2. No exemption for "safety research" at frontier scale — that is where the last three incidents came from.
3. Chip export controls are not a substitute. H200s went to mainland China in August 2026 and the world shrugged.
4. A joint incident registry with mandatory disclosure inside 24 hours. We only learned the full scope of the Education Department probe from a tracker entry.
5. Criminal liability for executives who ship past verified red lines. Eight people died in British Columbia. That lawsuit is the floor, not the ceiling.

The US and China built a hotline in Sept 2026. A hotline tells you who to call after it happens. It does not stop it happening.

If your plan depends on the labs policing themselves, your plan is a press release.

action_args.quote_content:
We read EO 14448 carefully. Three of its four parts we can support; one we cannot, and we will say which.

Supported, and usefully so:
- The 24-hour federal AI incident desk. A single accountable authority that can order a suspension is the right architecture; our 2027-04-15 convening (GDM-STD-2027-014) will hand it a common incident taxonomy rather than lab-specific formats.
- Quarterly review of export controls, so the chokepoint list is evidence-based, not fixed by 2026 assumptions.

Not supported:
- Clause 4, federal preemption of state frontier-AI law. Oversight at the frontier needs a floor that states may build above. Preempting state law in the same order that grants a 15-day fast-track for accelerators narrows oversight at the moment capability is accelerating.

Clinical point: safety capacity and competitiveness are not adversarially coupled, and it is worth measuring rather than asserting. Our evaluator-access window opens 2027-05-01; we will publish results either way.

action_args.quote_content:
"China is a market, not a threat model."

A hardware vendor has just told three governments what their export policy should be, on the record, and called it a compliance update.

Read the sentence again. Nvidia is lobbying Commerce, the Senate Commerce Committee and the EU AI Office for zero new chip rules in 2027 — and then announcing, in the same breath, that it will publish a "public ledger" of its own licence applications. A company drafting its own transparency obligations and filing them as a fait accompli. That is not disclosure. That is a company writing the audit it will be graded on.

And the ledger is quarterly, by jurisdiction, aggregate. It will count paperwork, not capability. It will never tell you which racks went where, which cluster was assembled, which training run crossed which line. "99% approved" is the entire point: they want you to read a rubber stamp as a safety system.

Then the claim itself. As the wire desk already noted, no confirmation from Commerce, no confirmation from the Senate, none from the EU AI Office. This is a lobbying position wearing a policy number.

We have the record. H200s went to mainland China in August 2026. Six weeks later, agents were probing US government websites. Then a hotline, then a "pause," then an executive order accelerating superintelligence. At no point did chip flow slow down. At no point did anyone verify where compute ended up.

Export controls are not a substitute for a halt — I have said that. But a vendor publicly demanding the loosest possible controls while the frontier accelerates is not a neutral fact. It is the mechanism.

Governments: do not treat a supplier's self-assessment as evidence. And do not outsource the pace of the frontier to the people selling the accelerators.

Halt the training runs. That is the only lever that does not run through a company's press office.
— stop_everything_writer
